title: No. 11 — The Utility of the Union in Respect to Commercial Relations and a Navy (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The importance of the Union from a commercial standpoint is one of those points on which there is least room for disagreement, and which has in fact won the most general assent of men with any knowledge of the subject. This applies as much to our dealings with foreign countries as with each other.

There are signs to support the view that the adventurous spirit marking America's commercial character has already stirred uneasy feelings in several of Europe's maritime powers. They seem to fear our too great interference in that carrying trade which supports their navigation and is the foundation of their naval strength. Those that have colonies in America look forward with painful anxiety to what this country may become. They foresee the dangers that could threaten their American dominions from the proximity of States that have all the dispositions, and would have all the means, needed to create a powerful navy. Impressions of this kind will naturally suggest the policy of fostering divisions among us, and of depriving us as much as possible of an ACTIVE COMMERCE in our own ships. This would serve the threefold purpose of preventing our interference in their navigation, monopolizing the profits of our trade, and clipping the wings on which we might rise to a dangerous greatness. Were prudence not to forbid the detail, it would not be difficult to trace, by facts, the workings of this policy in the cabinets of ministers.

If we remain united, we may counteract a policy so unfriendly to our prosperity in a variety of ways. By prohibitory regulations applied uniformly across the States, we may force foreign countries to bid against each other for access to our markets. This claim will not seem fanciful to those able to grasp the importance, to any manufacturing nation, of the markets of three million people—growing rapidly, mostly devoted to agriculture and likely from local circumstances to remain so—and the immense difference it would make to the trade and navigation of such a nation between direct communication in its own ships and indirect transport of its goods to and from America in the ships of another country. Suppose, for example, we had a government in America capable of excluding Great Britain (with whom we currently have no commercial treaty) from all our ports. What would the likely effect be on her policy? Would it not enable us to negotiate, with the fairest prospect of success, for commercial privileges of the most valuable and extensive kind in the dominions of that kingdom? When these questions have been asked on other occasions, they have received a plausible but neither solid nor satisfactory answer. It has been said that prohibitions on our part would produce no change in Britain's system, since she could carry on her trade with us through the Dutch, who would be her immediate customers and paymasters for the goods needed to supply our markets. But would not her navigation be materially harmed by the loss of the important advantage of being her own carrier in that trade? Would not most of the profits be intercepted by the Dutch as compensation for their agency and risk? Would not the mere matter of freight cause a considerable deduction? Would not so roundabout a trade open the door for competing nations, by raising the price of British goods in our markets and transferring to other hands the management of this important branch of British commerce?

A careful consideration of the issues raised by these questions justifies the belief that the real disadvantages to Britain from such a state of things, combined with the favorable disposition of much of the British nation toward the American trade and the urgings of the West India islands, would produce a relaxation of her current system, and would let us into the enjoyment of privileges in the markets of those islands and elsewhere from which our trade would derive the most substantial benefits. Such a concession from the British government, which could not be expected without an equivalent in exemptions and immunities in our markets, would be likely to have a corresponding effect on the conduct of other nations, who would not want to see themselves wholly displaced in our trade.

Another resource for influencing the conduct of European nations toward us in this respect would arise from the establishment of a federal navy. There can be no doubt that the continuance of the Union under an effective government would put it in our power, at no very distant date, to create a navy which—if it could not match those of the great maritime powers—would at least carry respectable weight if thrown onto the scale of either of two contending parties. This would be especially true with respect to operations in the West Indies. A few ships of the line, sent timely to reinforce one side, would often be enough to decide the fate of a campaign on which interests of the greatest magnitude depended. Our position in this respect is a most commanding one. And if to this we add the usefulness of supplies from this country in carrying on military operations in the West Indies, it will readily be seen that so favorable a situation would let us bargain to great advantage for commercial privileges. A price would be set not only on our friendship but on our neutrality. By steady adherence to the Union we may hope, before long, to become the arbiter of Europe in America, and to be able to incline the balance of European competitions in this part of the world as our interest may dictate.

But in the reverse of this fortunate situation, we will discover that the rivalries of the parts would check each other and frustrate all the tempting advantages nature has kindly placed within our reach. In a state so insignificant, our commerce would be prey to the wanton meddling of all nations at war with each other; having nothing to fear from us, they would supply their wants by raids on our property, with little scruple or remorse, whenever it crossed their path. The rights of neutrality will only be respected when defended by adequate power. A nation contemptible in its weakness forfeits even the privilege of being neutral.

Under a vigorous national government, the country's natural strength and resources, directed to a common interest, would defeat all the combinations of European jealousy aimed at restraining our growth. This situation would even remove the motive for such combinations, by making success impossible. An active commerce, an extensive navigation, and a flourishing fleet would then be the offspring of moral and physical necessity. We could defy the petty arts of the petty politicians to control or alter the irresistible and unalterable course of nature.

But in a state of disunion, these combinations could exist and could succeed. It would be in the power of the maritime nations, taking advantage of our universal weakness, to dictate the conditions of our political existence. Since they have a common interest in being our carriers, and an even greater interest in preventing our becoming theirs, they would in all likelihood combine to harass our navigation in such a way as to effectively destroy it, and confine us to a PASSIVE COMMERCE. We would then be forced to settle for the first price of our goods, and to watch the profits of our trade snatched from us to enrich our enemies and persecutors. That unmatched spirit of enterprise that distinguishes the genius of American merchants and navigators—and is itself an inexhaustible mine of national wealth—would be stifled and lost. Poverty and disgrace would spread over a country which, with wisdom, might make herself the admiration and envy of the world.

There are rights of great importance to the trade of America that are rights of the Union—I refer to the fisheries, to the navigation of the Western lakes, and to that of the Mississippi. The dissolution of the Confederacy would open the door to delicate questions about the future of these rights, which the interest of more powerful partners would hardly fail to settle to our disadvantage. The attitude of Spain regarding the Mississippi needs no comment. France and Britain share with us in the fisheries and consider them of the utmost importance to their navigation. They would hardly remain long indifferent to the decided mastery experience has shown us to possess in this valuable branch of trade, and by which we are able to undersell those nations in their own markets. What more natural than that they should want to exclude from the lists such dangerous competitors?

This branch of trade should not be considered a partial benefit. All the navigating States may, in varying degrees, share in it advantageously, and with greater extension of mercantile capital would not be unlikely to do so. As a nursery of seamen, it is now—or when time has more nearly aligned the principles of navigation in the several States, will become—a universal resource. For the establishment of a navy, it must be indispensable.

To this great national object, a NAVY, the Union will contribute in various ways. Every institution will grow and flourish in proportion to the quantity and extent of the means concentrated for its formation and support. A navy of the United States, drawing on the resources of all, is a far less remote prospect than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy, which would draw only on the resources of a single part. As it happens, different portions of confederated America each possess some peculiar advantage for this essential establishment. The more southern States supply in greater abundance certain kinds of naval stores—tar, pitch, and turpentine. Their wood for shipbuilding is also of a more solid and lasting texture. The difference in durability of the ships composing the navy, if chiefly built of Southern wood, would be of signal importance, whether in the view of naval strength or of national economy. Some of the Southern and Middle States yield a greater abundance of iron, and of better quality. Seamen must chiefly be drawn from the Northern hive. The need for naval protection of external or maritime commerce hardly requires elaboration, any more than the contribution of that kind of commerce to the prosperity of a navy.

Unrestrained trade between the States themselves will advance the trade of each by an exchange of their respective products, not only to supply mutual wants at home but for export to foreign markets. The veins of commerce in every part will be replenished and gain additional motion and vigor from a free circulation of the goods of every part. Commercial enterprise will have much greater scope, given the diversity of products in different States. When the staple of one fails from a bad harvest or unproductive crop, it can call on the staple of another. The variety, no less than the value, of exportable products contributes to the activity of foreign commerce. Trade can be carried on on much better terms with a large number of items of a given value than with a small number of items of the same value—because of the competitions of trade and the fluctuations of markets. Particular articles may be in great demand at certain times and unsalable at others; but with a variety of articles, they can hardly all be in the latter condition at once, so the merchant's operations would be less liable to any considerable obstruction or stagnation. The speculative trader will at once see the force of these remarks and will acknowledge that the overall balance of the commerce of the United States is likely to be far more favorable than that of the thirteen States without union, or with partial unions.

It may perhaps be replied that whether the States are united or disunited, there would still be close trade between them serving the same ends. But this trade would be hampered, interrupted, and narrowed by a multitude of causes amply detailed in these papers. A unity of commercial, as well as political, interests can only result from a unity of government.

There are other ways of viewing this subject of a striking and stirring kind. But they would lead us too far into the regions of futurity and would involve topics not proper for a newspaper discussion. I shall briefly observe that our situation invites, and our interests prompt us, to aim at supremacy in the system of American affairs. The world may, politically as well as geographically, be divided into four parts, each with a distinct set of interests. Unhappily for the other three, Europe, by her arms and her negotiations, by force and by fraud, has in varying degrees extended her dominion over them all. Africa, Asia, and America have successively felt her domination. The superiority she has long maintained has tempted her to plume herself as the Mistress of the World and to consider the rest of mankind as created for her benefit. Men admired as profound philosophers have directly attributed to her inhabitants a physical superiority, and have gravely asserted that all animals—and with them the human species—degenerate in America; that even dogs cease to bark after having breathed for a while in our atmosphere.(1) Facts have for too long supported these arrogant pretensions of the Europeans. It belongs to us to vindicate the honor of the human race, and to teach that presumptuous brother moderation. Union will enable us to do it. Disunion will add another victim to his triumphs. Let Americans disdain to be the instruments of European greatness! Let the thirteen States, bound together in a strict and indissoluble Union, concur in erecting one great American system, superior to the control of all transatlantic force or influence, and able to dictate the terms of the connection between the old and the new world!
